passage:
Someone had posted that Jaya's small bakery sold stale cakes and cheated customers. The lie travelled fast, and by Monday her phone was full of angry replies. Her stomach knotted, but she did not answer one.

Instead, she took screenshots with the date and time, saved the links in a folder, and wrote down which claims were false and how she knew. On Tuesday she used the platform's help form to report the posts. Then she booked an hour with Bhavna, an advocate, who read the folder patiently and explained what options existed and how long they usually take.

Jaya did not write back angrily, though she badly wanted to. She had a plan now, and it was slow and steady.

qa.a: Jaya felt anxious and hurt, shown by her knotted stomach, but she held back from reacting.

qa.a: Bhavna would probably see organised evidence that makes the case easier to assess, and that Jaya wants a lawful route rather than a fight.

"They're saying I stole money from the club," Bhupen said, laptop open on the dining table. "It's a lie, and it's everywhere."
His sister Keerthana pulled up a chair. "Don't reply. Did you save it?"
"Every post, with dates. Forty-one screenshots in one folder."
"Good. What next?"
"The platform has a form for false claims. I filled it last night with the links." He scrolled. "They took down two posts this morning, not the rest."
"And the lawyer Appa mentioned?"
"Mrs Rao. I have a call at four. I've written my questions: what options exist, what she needs from me, and whether any of my own posts could make it worse."
"You're not going to post back?"
"No. If I fight online, it becomes my word against theirs in public. I want it handled properly."
Keerthana squeezed his shoulder. "I'll sit in on the call."

qa.a: He had saved forty-one screenshots in one folder.

When the posts claiming I'd faked my internship certificate started spreading, my first instinct was to write a furious thread naming everyone involved. My flatmate Joseph talked me out of it in about four sentences.
Instead I did three things. First, I saved everything: every post, every share, every comment with a date, into one spreadsheet with links. Second, I used the platform's reporting form for false information and attached the actual certificate and the company's confirmation email. That got most posts removed within a week.
Third, the main account kept reposting, so I booked a consultation through my college's legal aid clinic. The advocate there read my file and explained what options existed and what each would involve. I haven't decided yet whether to go further.
I never replied publicly once. I'm Anirban, and it was the hardest silence I've ever kept.

qa.q: What did Anirban attach to the platform report?
qa.a: Anirban attached the actual certificate and the company's confirmation email.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when the posts first spread?
qa.a: Anirban felt furious and wanted to write a thread naming everyone, and later found staying silent very hard.

qa.q: What else could Anirban do while deciding about further steps?
qa.a: Anirban could keep the spreadsheet updated and ask the advocate what new evidence would matter, so any later choice rests on a full record.

qa.q: How might Joseph see the way Anirban handled it?
qa.a: Joseph, who talked Anirban out of the furious thread, would likely feel relieved that the problem was handled through reports and advice instead of a public fight.

grounding: Shows the person keeping records and using the platform's reporting process and a legal aid consultation, pursuing lawful remedies without retaliation.
